questions.q: What is the defining condition for a matrix U to be unitary?
options: U^dagger U = I, meaning U's conjugate transpose is also its inverse
U = U^dagger, meaning U equals its own conjugate transpose
The determinant of U must equal zero
Every entry of U must be a real number between 0 and 1
questions.explain: Unitary means U^dagger U = I (equivalently U U^dagger = I) -- the conjugate transpose serves as the matrix's inverse. 'U = U^dagger' is the definition of Hermitian, a different (though related) property.

questions.q: For the Hadamard matrix H = (1/sqrt(2))[[1,1],[1,-1]], computing H^dagger H gives which result, confirming it is unitary?
options: The identity matrix [[1,0],[0,1]]
2 times the identity matrix, [[2,0],[0,2]]
The zero matrix [[0,0],[0,0]]
H itself, unchanged
questions.explain: Working out H^dagger H entry by entry (using H^dagger = H since H is real and symmetric) gives exactly [[1,0],[0,1]] = I, confirming H is unitary.

questions.q: Why do unitary matrices preserve the norm of any vector they act on?
options: Because <Up|Uq> = p^dagger U^dagger U q = p^dagger I q = <p|q>, so setting q=p shows ||Up|| = ||p|| exactly
Because unitary matrices always have determinant equal to 1
Because unitary matrices only ever contain real number entries
Norm preservation is simply assumed by definition, with no underlying reason
questions.explain: The inner product of two transformed vectors reduces to the inner product of the originals because U^dagger U = I cancels out. Setting the two vectors equal shows the norm itself is preserved.

questions.q: Why must every quantum gate be represented by a unitary matrix?
options: Quantum evolution must be reversible (unitary's inverse is always U^dagger) and must preserve a state's norm so total measurement probability still sums to 1 after the gate is applied
Unitary matrices are simply easier to multiply together than other matrices
Because all quantum gates must have every entry equal to a real number
Because unitary matrices always have the same effect as the identity matrix
questions.explain: Two physical requirements force this: evolution must be undoable (guaranteed since U^dagger is always U's inverse), and a valid state's norm of 1 must be preserved so probabilities still sum to 1 after the gate -- unitary matrices are exactly the matrices satisfying both.

questions.q: The matrix N = [[1, i], [i, 1]] (without a normalizing factor) satisfies N^dagger N = 2I rather than I. What does this tell you?
options: N is not unitary, even though its structure resembles a unitary matrix -- the missing normalization factor breaks the U^dagger U = I condition
N is unitary, since 2I is considered equivalent to I for this purpose
N must be Hermitian instead, since it fails the unitary test
The calculation is irrelevant because N has complex entries
questions.explain: Unitary requires U^dagger U to equal exactly I, not any scalar multiple of I. N^dagger N = 2I means N is not unitary -- a reminder to always verify the exact identity rather than assuming a plausible-looking matrix qualifies.
